Frogs
FROGZ
noun (plural)
From the Saxon frogga, an amphibious creature of the marsh; rendering the Hebrew tsephardea', the frog of the Nile, and the Greek batrachos in the vision of the Apocalypse.

Biblical Definition

The frogs are the second plague of Egypt and, at the end of the Bible, the likeness of three unclean spirits. The LORD warned Pharaoh, “if thou refuse to let them go, behold, I will smite all thy borders with frogs” (Exo 8:2), and when Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters “the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt” (Exo 8:6). The psalm remembers where they went: “their land brought forth frogs in abundance, in the chambers of their kings” (Psa 105:30). Nothing was exempt, not the bedchamber of Pharaoh himself. The stroke fell on Egypt’s religion as well as its comfort, for the frog was a sacred creature of the Nile, emblem of the goddess of fruitfulness; the LORD gave Egypt its deity in such quantity that it became a torment. And He gave Moses the sign of His mastery in the timing: Pharaoh himself named the hour, and “the LORD did according to the word of Moses; and the frogs died out of the houses” (Exo 8:13). A god that can be summoned by an Egyptian magician is no god; a God who removes the plague at an appointed minute is the Lord of it. The image returns in Rev 16:13, where John sees “three unclean spirits like frogs” issuing from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — lying words swarming out of the mouth, croaking in every chamber, gathering the kings of the earth to the battle of the great day.

Webster 1828 Definition

Amphibious creatures of the marsh; the second plague of Egypt, and in the Apocalypse the likeness of unclean spirits of deceit.

FROG, an amphibious animal of the marsh, remarkable for leaping and for its croaking.

From the Saxon frogga.

Renders the Hebrew tsephardea' and the Greek batrachos.

The second of the ten plagues upon Egypt (Exo 8:2-14).

In Rev 16:13, the likeness under which three unclean spirits are seen.

Key Scripture

Exo 8:2 — "And if thou refuse to let them go, behold, I will smite all thy borders with frogs:"

Exo 8:6 — "And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt."

Psa 105:30 — "Their land brought forth frogs in abundance, in the chambers of their kings."

Rev 16:13 — "And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet."

Modern Corruption

The second plague is dissolved into a natural chain of river events, and the frogs of Rev 16:13 are treated as scenery rather than as lying doctrine.

expand to see more

The frogs are the hinge of the naturalising retelling of the Exodus: a fouled Nile drives the frogs ashore, the frogs die, and the rest of the plagues follow as consequences. It is presented as respect for the text and it is a quiet denial of it, for the narrative does not describe frogs fleeing a river — it describes frogs coming up at the stretching out of a rod, filling the ovens and the kneadingtroughs and the bedchamber of the king, and dying at an hour Pharaoh himself appointed (Exo 8:9-13). A natural chain has no appointments. The plagues are neither folklore nor mythological elements imported into the record; they are history, ten deliberate strokes against Egypt’s gods, and the frog — sacred to Egypt — was chosen with the same precision as every other.

The second corruption is to read Rev 16:13 as mere grotesque imagery. John was shown something exact. The unclean spirits are like frogs, and they come out of the mouth: the emblem is croaking, ceaseless, everywhere at once, filling every chamber, impossible to shut out. That is the character of the world’s deceiving doctrine at the end — not chiefly violent but vocal, multiplying faster than it can be answered, and issuing from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet, which is to say from Satan, from political power, and from corrupted religion. The believer’s defence is not a louder croak but the word of God, and the blessing set in the very next verse upon the man who watches and keeps his garments.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The second plague of Egypt, and the emblem in the Apocalypse of unclean spirits issuing from the mouth.

expand to see more

Frog — Saxon frogga; Hebrew tsephardea'; Greek batrachos.

Exo 8:2-6: frogs cover the land of Egypt at the stretching out of Aaron’s hand.

Psa 105:30: they reach the chambers of the kings — no rank exempted.

Exo 8:13: they die at the hour Pharaoh named — the LORD masters the plague He sent.

Rev 16:13: three unclean spirits like frogs out of the mouths of dragon, beast and false prophet.

Usage

"Egypt’s sacred frog was given to Egypt in such abundance that it became a torment."

"The frogs died at the hour Pharaoh named — that timing is the whole argument."

"Frogs out of the mouth: the end-time deception is vocal, ceaseless, and everywhere."
